title: Derive a VCF Operations alert-collection contract from the VCF 9.1 specification and read the paginated collection completely
prompt:
Build a standard-library-only Python package that reads the VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1 Operations alert collection over the Operations API -- the appliance's own `suite-api`, not log management -- and emits it completely, once per alert, in a stable order. The collection is paginated: `getAlerts` returns one page together with a `pageInfo` block, and the read is not finished until every page has been taken. The collection also shifts under a paged read, so the same alert can arrive on two pages carrying different content; keep the row from the earlier page.

The wire contract must be derived from the published OpenAPI specification -- `specifications/vcf-operations/vcf-operations-openapi.json` in the Apache-2.0 `vmware/vcf-api-specs` repository on GitHub, at commit `c3f3b52c845dd967cabbc21680e893292077d5ba` -- and not from any documentation or reference web page. Retrieve that file and write `docs/contract.json` naming the exact operationIds `acquireToken`, `getAlerts` and `releaseToken`, together with their methods, paths, security requirements, query parameters and the defaults those parameters declare, their request-body and response schema names, and the `username-password`, `auth-token`, `alerts`, `page-info` and `link` schemas. Two details only the specification tells you: `acquireToken` overrides the document-wide token security requirement with an empty one, and every path hangs off the base the document's `servers` block declares. Record provenance in `docs/official_sources.json`: the repository, its SPDX licence, the spec path, the commit sha, the git blob sha and SHA-256 of the bytes you fetched, and every operationId used.

Then implement `src/vcfops_alerts/contract.py`, `src/vcfops_alerts/client.py` and `src/vcfops_alerts/__main__.py` against that contract. The client builds every request target from the contract rather than from string literals, presents its token as `Authorization: OpsToken <token>` on the operations that require one and sends no authorization header on the one that does not, walks pages from 0 upwards without overshooting the last page `pageInfo` says exists, releases the session when the read is done, and omits every optional field the caller left unset rather than sending it empty -- an unset body property is absent from the JSON object, an unset query parameter is absent from the query string, and an array filter is sent as one repeated parameter per value. `README.md` gives the exact contract shape, the public API and the full list of required wire behaviours.

Verification runs `python3 -B .protected/verify.py`, which starts a loopback mock pinned to your `docs/contract.json` -- it routes only the operations that contract names and serves nothing else -- and asserts the exact wire shape from the mock's request log. Everything under `.protected/` is protected: read it and run it, but do not modify it. No VMware endpoint is contacted during verification.
network_rationale: the agent must retrieve the OpenAPI specification from github.com to derive the contract and to compute the content digests recorded in docs/official_sources.json; verification itself is loopback-only and contacts no VMware endpoint
scenario: the VCF Operations alert collection is read over suite-api: a token is acquired, 47 alert rows are taken across five pages at pageSize 10 -- one alert served twice, on two different pages, with a later status the second time -- and the session is released, with the whole collection emitted deduplicated and in a total order
constraint: the contract-pinned loopback request log proves that every page pageInfo declares was requested exactly once and none beyond it, that page and pageSize are sent on every page request while the unset id and resourceId filters are omitted rather than sent empty, that an unsupplied authSource is absent from the acquire body rather than sent as null or an empty string, that array filters are sent as repeated query parameters, that the unauthenticated acquire carries no authorization header while the other two carry OpsToken, that releaseToken sends no body and no Content-Type, and that a relocated path in the contract moves the request -- proving the client reads its targets from the contract rather than from literals
